lesson.title: Port Numbers: Sorting Traffic to the Right Application
lesson.summary: Explains the port number as the value that identifies a specific application or process on a host, allowing many simultaneous conversations to share a single IP address.
lesson.body:
An IP address gets a packet to the correct network interface, but that alone does not finish the job. A single host might be running a web browser, an email client, and a video call all at the same time, each one sending and receiving its own separate stream of data through the very same interface and the very same IP address. Something has to sort incoming data to the correct application once it arrives, and that something is the port number. A port number is a 16-bit value, ranging from 0 to 65535, that identifies a specific process or application running on a host, working alongside the host's IP address to fully specify exactly where a piece of data is headed.

Together, an IP address and a port number form what is often called a socket address, typically written as the IP address followed by a colon and the port, for example 203.0.113.5:443. This pairing is what allows a single interface, with a single IP address, to support many independent conversations simultaneously. Each conversation is distinguished not by using a different IP address, but by using a different combination of ports on each end, a technique often described as multiplexing, since many separate streams are combined onto the same underlying connection point and then correctly separated back out, or demultiplexed, when they arrive.

Certain port numbers are reserved by convention for specific, well-known services, so that a client does not need to guess which port a server is listening on. Ports 0 through 1023 are known as well-known ports and are assigned to common services: web traffic conventionally uses port 80 for unencrypted connections and port 443 for encrypted connections, domain name lookups use port 53, and secure remote login uses port 22. A server generally listens on the well-known port associated with its service, while a client connecting to that server typically uses a temporary, less predictable port number of its own for that one conversation.

Consider a worked example that completes the picture built across this entire chapter. Suppose you open two browser tabs and load two different pages from the very same web server at the same time. Both requests leave your laptop through the same network interface, using the same IP address, and both are addressed to the same server IP address on port 443, since both are secure web traffic. What keeps the two page loads from being confused with each other is that your laptop assigns each browser tab a different temporary source port number of its own. The server sees two separate conversations, distinguished by their different source ports, even though both share the same source and destination IP addresses and the same destination port.

Port numbers are the final piece that makes modern networking practical at the scale it operates today: without them, every application on a host would need its own IP address just to hold a separate conversation, which would be enormously wasteful. Instead, a single interface with a single IP address, the concepts covered earlier in this chapter, can support an essentially unlimited number of simultaneous conversations, each cleanly sorted to the right application by nothing more than a small number attached to each end of the exchange.
